analysis.one_liner: Bans unlimited 'soft money' contributions to national political parties and tightens campaign finance disclosure.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 252-177 in September 1999, but it never got a vote in the Senate and died when that Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have stopped national political parties from raising and spending 'soft money' — unlimited donations from corporations, unions, and wealthy individuals that sit outside normal contribution limits. It would have forced campaign reports onto the internet within 24 hours, made more ads count as campaign ads, doubled penalties for violations, and barred fundraising inside federal buildings. It also raised the individual giving cap from $25,000 to $30,000 and added union dues notice rules, provisions added to win votes.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters gain the most: the main route parties used to collect six- and seven-figure checks from corporations, unions, and wealthy donors would close, and campaigns would have to disclose money faster and in public view online. Small donors get somewhat more weight relative to big checks. Federal officeholders and the White House lose the ability to raise money on federal property or trade access to government planes and rooms for donations.

how_it_helps.text: National party committees could no longer solicit, receive, or spend money outside the federal contribution limits, closing the 'soft money' channel used for unlimited donations [S2][S4].
The FEC would have to post electronically filed campaign reports on the internet within 24 hours, and campaigns could not deposit contributions missing required donor information [S2][S4].
Candidates and outside groups would face clear rules on when an ad counts as a campaign ad, plus 24- and 48-hour reporting of big independent expenditures right before elections [S2][S4].

Fundraising on federal property would carry criminal penalties, and parties would have to repay the government at commercial rates when the President or Vice President uses Air Force One for a fundraiser [S2][S4].

Penalties for knowing campaign law violations would double, mandatory fines would apply to late filings, and knowingly violating reporting rules for $2,000 or more could bring one to ten years in prison [S2][S4].

analysis.who_pays: National party committees and the corporations, unions, and wealthy individuals who give them unregulated money lose the soft money channel and face tighter reporting, faster deadlines, and doubled penalties. Wealthy self-funded candidates gain an incentive to limit their own spending. Incumbents lose the ability to send taxpayer-funded mass mailings in the months before an election.

drawbacks.text: The bill raised the aggregate individual contribution limit from $25,000 to $30,000, letting the biggest donors give more [S2][S3].

It codified the Supreme Court's Beck decision, requiring unions to give nonmember employees a way to reduce payments used for politics — a provision critics called an attack on union political activity, though supporters said it protects workers' paychecks [S2][S3].

Its definition of a campaign ad leaned on specific phrases like 'vote for' or 'defeat', and even included a carve-out saying background music without lyrics cannot make an ad count — leaving room for ads that attack candidates without those exact words to escape the rules [S4].
It did not provide public financing or address independent 'issue advocacy' ads comprehensively; enforcement still ran through the FEC, whose existing weakness the bill only partly fixed [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: closing soft money cuts the largest, least traceable money in politics, at the cost of party committees' fundraising flexibility and some union political funds. The disclosure and enforcement upgrades benefit everyone regardless of party. The union dues provision was a political sweetener rather than a campaign finance necessity, and the ad-definition loopholes mean the bill would not have caught everything. On balance it was a genuine, if imperfect, reform with modest costs to concentrated money.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 252-177, but the Senate sent it to its Rules Committee in September 1999 and it sat there with no vote until that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 19, 1999 and referred to six House committees at once [S6].
The House Committee on House Administration considered it and reported it adversely — a formal recommendation against the bill — on August 5, 1999 [S6].
Supporters got the bill pulled from the other committees onto the House calendar and then to the floor under a rule, showing it could win despite committee resistance [S6].
On September 14, 1999 the House passed the bill 252-177: 197 of 211 voting Democrats and 54 of 222 voting Republicans in favor [S7].
The Senate received the bill on September 16 and referred it to the Committee on Rules and Administration on September 29, 1999; no further Senate action is recorded [S6].
The 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, and the bill died in committee without a Senate vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: National party committees and the large donors behind them came out ahead: unlimited soft money stayed legal and largely undisclosed for the 2000 elections and beyond. Incumbents who relied on it were also better off than they would have been under the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Democrats backed the bill almost unanimously (197-13), while most Republicans opposed it (164 no, 54 yes) — a bipartisan-sponsored bill that split sharply by party in the final vote [S7].

industries.note: The bill bans national parties from soliciting or spending soft money — unlimited donations outside federal limits — cutting off their largest unregulated funding stream. That money paid for ads and voter drives that primarily served party and donor interests.

industries.industry: Large donors, corporations, and wealthy individuals
industries.note: They would lose the ability to give unlimited soft money to national parties, though the bill slightly raised the total they could give through regular channels, from $25,000 to $30,000.

The bill codifies the Beck decision, forcing unions to let nonmember employees reduce payments used for political activity. Unions lose political funds and a direct fundraising ban on parties applies to them too, though the notice rules give workers control over their own payments.
Party committees would be barred from soliciting or routing money to tax-exempt groups, closing a channel that let big donations fund campaigns without appearing on any federal report.
